claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations from previous studies.

claims.claim: gp78 associates with Insig-1 in a sterol-independent manner.
claims.source: However, gp78 was reported to be responsible for the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR as (i) gp78 associates with Insig-1 in a sterol-independent manner, (ii) Insig-1 mediates a sterol-dependent interaction between HMGCR and gp78, (iii) overexpression of the transmembrane domains of gp78 exerted a dominant-negative effect and inhibited HMGCR degradation, and (iv), siRNA-mediated depletion of gp78 resulted in decreased sterol-induced ubiquitination and degradation of HMGCR (Song et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from a previous study.

claims.claim: Insig-1 mediates a sterol-dependent interaction between HMGCR and gp78.
claims.source: However, gp78 was reported to be responsible for the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR as (i) gp78 associates with Insig-1 in a sterol-independent manner, (ii) Insig-1 mediates a sterol-dependent interaction between HMGCR and gp78, (iii) overexpression of the transmembrane domains of gp78 exerted a dominant-negative effect and inhibited HMGCR degradation, and (iv), siRNA-mediated depletion of gp78 resulted in decreased sterol-induced ubiquitination and degradation of HMGCR (Song et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from a previous study.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the transmembrane domains of gp78 inhibited HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: However, gp78 was reported to be responsible for the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR as (i) gp78 associates with Insig-1 in a sterol-independent manner, (ii) Insig-1 mediates a sterol-dependent interaction between HMGCR and gp78, (iii) overexpression of the transmembrane domains of gp78 exerted a dominant-negative effect and inhibited HMGCR degradation, and (iv), siRNA-mediated depletion of gp78 resulted in decreased sterol-induced ubiquitination and degradation of HMGCR (Song et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from a previous study.

claims.claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of gp78 resulted in decreased sterol-induced ubiquitination and degradation of HMGCR.
claims.source: However, gp78 was reported to be responsible for the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR as (i) gp78 associates with Insig-1 in a sterol-independent manner, (ii) Insig-1 mediates a sterol-dependent interaction between HMGCR and gp78, (iii) overexpression of the transmembrane domains of gp78 exerted a dominant-negative effect and inhibited HMGCR degradation, and (iv), siRNA-mediated depletion of gp78 resulted in decreased sterol-induced ubiquitination and degradation of HMGCR (Song et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from a previous study.

claims.claim: TRC8 is involved in HMGCR degradation in addition to gp78.
claims.source: The same laboratory subsequently suggested that the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR was mediated by two ERAD E3 ubiquitin ligases, with TRC8 involved in addition to gp78 (Jo et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from a previous study.

claims.claim: An independent study found no evidence for either gp78 or TRC8 in the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR.
claims.source: However, these findings remain controversial as, despite confirming a role for gp78 in the regulation of Insig-1 (Lee et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2012), an independent study found no evidence for either gp78 or TRC8 in the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR (Tsai et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from a previous study.

claims.claim: Clover was fused to the C-terminus of endogenous HMGCR to generate an HMGCR-Clover fusion protein.
claims.source: To identify genes involved in the post-translational regulation of HMGCR, we engineered a cell line in which Clover, a bright fluorescent protein (Lam et al., 2012), was fused to the C-terminus of endogenous HMGCR, generating an HMGCR-Clover fusion protein (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Basal HMGCR-Clover levels in sterol-replete tissue culture media were undetectable by flow cytometry.
claims.source: Basal HMGCR-Clover levels in sterol-replete tissue culture media were undetectable by flow cytometry (Figure 1B) and phenocopy endogenous WT HMGCR expression (Figure 1C, compare lanes 1 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claims.claim: Following overnight sterol depletion, a ~25 fold increase in HMGCR-Clover expression was detected.
claims.source: Following overnight sterol depletion, a ~ 25 fold increase in HMGCR-Clover expression was detected (shaded grey to blue histogram in Figure 1D, Figure 1C (lanes 2 and 5)), representing a combination of increased SREBP-induced transcription and decreased sterol-induced HMGCR degradation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D and 1C.

claims.claim: Reintroduction of sterols induced the rapid degradation of HMGCR-Clover (~80% decrease within 2 hr).
claims.source: Reintroduction of sterols induced the rapid degradation of HMGCR-Clover (~80% decrease within 2 hr), confirming the sterol-dependent regulation of the reporter (blue to red histogram in Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: At least one HMGCR allele remained untagged in the reporter cells.
claims.source: Residual, untagged HMGCR detected by immunoblot analysis in the reporter cells under sterol-depleted conditions suggested that at least one HMGCR allele remained untagged (Figure 1C, compare lanes 2 and 5), which was confirmed by PCR-amplification and sequencing of the genomic locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: Inhibiting the enzymatic activity of HMGCR with mevastatin stabilised HMGCR-Clover expression.
claims.source: Inhibiting the enzymatic activity of HMGCR with mevastatin also stabilised HMGCR-Clover expression, as did inhibition of the proteasome (bortezomib) or p97/VCP (NMS-873) (Figure 1E), confirming the rapid, steady-state degradation of the HMGCR reporter.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Inhibition of the proteasome with bortezomib stabilised HMGCR-Clover expression.
claims.source: Inhibiting the enzymatic activity of HMGCR with mevastatin also stabilised HMGCR-Clover expression, as did inhibition of the proteasome (bortezomib) or p97/VCP (NMS-873) (Figure 1E), confirming the rapid, steady-state degradation of the HMGCR reporter.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Inhibition of p97/VCP with NMS-873 stabilised HMGCR-Clover expression.
claims.source: Inhibiting the enzymatic activity of HMGCR with mevastatin also stabilised HMGCR-Clover expression, as did inhibition of the proteasome (bortezomib) or p97/VCP (NMS-873) (Figure 1E), confirming the rapid, steady-state degradation of the HMGCR reporter.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated ablation of both Insig-1 and −2 together induced a dramatic increase in HMGCR-Clover expression.
claims.source: Furthermore, we showed that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated ablation of both Insig-1 and −2 together induced a dramatic increase in HMGCR-Clover expression, equivalent to levels seen following sterol depletion (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: CRISPR-mediated gene disruption of either Insig-1 or −2 alone caused only a small, steady-state rescue of HMGCR-Clover.
claims.source: CRISPR-mediated gene disruption of either Insig-1 or −2 alone caused only a small, steady-state rescue of HMGCR-Clover (Figure 1F), which was more pronounced with the loss of Insig-1 than Insig-2.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Insig-1-deficient cells were unable to completely degrade HMGCR upon sterol addition.
claims.source: While Insig-1-deficient cells were unable to completely degrade HMGCR upon sterol addition, only a minor defect in HMGCR degradation was seen in the absence of Insig-2 (Figure 1F), suggesting that Insig-1 is dominant over Insig-2 under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Only a minor defect in HMGCR degradation was seen in the absence of Insig-2.
claims.source: While Insig-1-deficient cells were unable to completely degrade HMGCR upon sterol addition, only a minor defect in HMGCR degradation was seen in the absence of Insig-2 (Figure 1F), suggesting that Insig-1 is dominant over Insig-2 under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Insig-1 is dominant over Insig-2 under these conditions.
claims.source: While Insig-1-deficient cells were unable to completely degrade HMGCR upon sterol addition, only a minor defect in HMGCR degradation was seen in the absence of Insig-2 (Figure 1F), suggesting that Insig-1 is dominant over Insig-2 under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: HMGCR-Clover was appropriately localised to the ER.
claims.source: Finally, we confirmed that HMGCR-Clover was appropriately localised to the ER by confocal microscopy (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: A genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen identified RNF145 as an E3 ligase required for HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: To identify genes required for the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen in HMGCR-Clover cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The genome-wide screen identified UBE2G2 as required for HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: The screen identified the E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme UBE2G2 and its accessory factor AUP1, which recruits UBE2G2 to lipid droplets and membrane E3 ubiquitin ligases (Klemm et al., 2011; Jo et al., 2013; Spandl et al., 2011; Christianson et al., 2011), as well as both Insig-1 and −2 (Yabe et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Sever et al., 2003a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The genome-wide screen identified AUP1 as required for HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: The screen identified the E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme UBE2G2 and its accessory factor AUP1, which recruits UBE2G2 to lipid droplets and membrane E3 ubiquitin ligases (Klemm et al., 2011; Jo et al., 2013; Spandl et al., 2011; Christianson et al., 2011), as well as both Insig-1 and −2 (Yabe et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Sever et al., 2003a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: AUP1 recruits UBE2G2 to lipid droplets and membrane E3 ubiquitin ligases.
claims.source: The screen identified the E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme UBE2G2 and its accessory factor AUP1, which recruits UBE2G2 to lipid droplets and membrane E3 ubiquitin ligases (Klemm et al., 2011; Jo et al., 2013; Spandl et al., 2011; Christianson et al., 2011), as well as both Insig-1 and −2 (Yabe et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Sever et al., 2003a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The genome-wide screen identified both Insig-1 and −2 as required for HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: The screen identified the E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme UBE2G2 and its accessory factor AUP1, which recruits UBE2G2 to lipid droplets and membrane E3 ubiquitin ligases (Klemm et al., 2011; Jo et al., 2013; Spandl et al., 2011; Christianson et al., 2011), as well as both Insig-1 and −2 (Yabe et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Sever et al., 2003a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: RNF145 shares 27% amino acid identity with TRC8.
claims.source: Strikingly, the only ER-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase to emerge from the screen is the poorly characterised RNF145. RNF145 shares 27% amino acid identity with TRC8, which is one of the E3 ligases (together with gp78) previously suggested to ubiquitinate HMGCR (Jo et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claims.claim: RNF145 harbours a YLYF motif at its N-terminus.
claims.source: Interestingly, RNF145 also harbours a YLYF motif at its N-terminus, which is similar to the YIYF motif present in the sterol-sensing domain (SSD) of SCAP and HMGCR required for their binding to the Insig proteins (Yang et al., 2002; Sever et al., 2003a; Jiang et al., 2018; Cook et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The YLYF motif in RNF145 is similar to the YIYF motif present in the sterol-sensing domain of SCAP and HMGCR.
claims.source: Interestingly, RNF145 also harbours a YLYF motif at its N-terminus, which is similar to the YIYF motif present in the sterol-sensing domain (SSD) of SCAP and HMGCR required for their binding to the Insig proteins (Yang et al., 2002; Sever et al., 2003a; Jiang et al., 2018; Cook et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The YIYF motif in SCAP and HMGCR is required for their binding to the Insig proteins.
claims.source: Interestingly, RNF145 also harbours a YLYF motif at its N-terminus, which is similar to the YIYF motif present in the sterol-sensing domain (SSD) of SCAP and HMGCR required for their binding to the Insig proteins (Yang et al., 2002; Sever et al., 2003a; Jiang et al., 2018; Cook et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Depletion of RNF145 caused a small and highly reproducible decrease in HMGCR-Clover degradation following re-introduction of sterols.
claims.source: Under cholesterol-replete conditions, no accumulation of the HMGCR-reporter was observed in RNF145-depleted cells (top and middle rows, Figure 2D), but a small and highly reproducible decrease in HMGCR-Clover degradation was seen following re-introduction of sterols (red histograms, bottom row in Figure 2D), emphasising the utility of the endogenous fluorescent reporter in identifying subtle phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The modest effect of RNF145 loss on HMGCR-Clover sterol-induced degradation suggested the involvement of additional ligase(s).
claims.source: Since the identity of the E3 ubiquitin ligases regulating HMGCR turnover remains controversial, the modest effect of RNF145 loss on HMGCR-Clover sterol-induced degradation suggested the involvement of additional ligase(s).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: A ubiquitome-targeted CRISPR/Cas9 screen in RNF145-deficient cells identified gp78 as required for HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: Strikingly, this screen identified gp78 (gene name: AMFR) (Figure 3B, Table 2), the E3 ubiquitin ligase previously implicated in HMGCR degradation (Jo et al., 2011; Song et al., 2005; Fang et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: There was no difference in sterol-induced HMGCR-Clover degradation between control and gp78-depleted HMGCR-Clover cells.
claims.source: Taking a combined knockout strategy we asked whether gp78 and RNF145 are together responsible for HMGCR degradation. As predicted by the genetic approach (Figure 3C (ii)), there was no difference in sterol-induced HMGCR-Clover degradation between control and gp78-depleted HMGCR-Clover cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Gp78 was not a false-negative from the initial genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen.
claims.source: Gp78 was not, therefore, a false-negative from our initial, genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: Sterol-induced HMGCR-Clover degradation was mildly impaired in RNF145-depleted cells.
claims.source: Individual knockout of RNF145 again showed that sterol-induced HMGCR-Clover degradation was mildly impaired in RNF145-depleted cells (Figure 3C (iii)).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: sgRNA-mediated targeting of gp78 together with RNF145 resulted in a significant increase in both steady-state HMGCR-Clover and an inability to degrade HMGCR-Clover upon addition of sterols.
claims.source: However, sgRNA-mediated targeting of gp78 together with RNF145 (Figure 3C (iv), see Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B lane three for knockout validation), resulted in a significant increase in both steady-state HMGCR-Clover (Figure 3C (iv) grey to green filled histograms) and an inability to degrade HMGCR-Clover upon addition of sterols to sterol-starved cells (Figure 3C (iv) blue to red histogram), a phenotype comparable to UBE2G2 deletion (Figure 3C (v)).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: RNF145 and gp78 are partially functionally redundant.
claims.source: Our results therefore suggest a partial functional redundancy between gp78 and RNF145 and imply that both ligases can independently regulate the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: Both RNF145 and gp78 can independently regulate the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR.
claims.source: Our results therefore suggest a partial functional redundancy between gp78 and RNF145 and imply that both ligases can independently regulate the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: Loss of gp78 alone did not affect HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: Similarly, loss of gp78 alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A for sgRNA validation) did not affect HMGCR degradation (Figure 3D, compare lanes 6 and 7–10), but loss of gp78 together with RNF145 resulted in a significant rescue of steady state HMGCR (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Loss of gp78 together with RNF145 resulted in a significant rescue of steady state HMGCR.
claims.source: Similarly, loss of gp78 alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A for sgRNA validation) did not affect HMGCR degradation (Figure 3D, compare lanes 6 and 7–10), but loss of gp78 together with RNF145 resulted in a significant rescue of steady state HMGCR (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: gp78/RNF145 double-knockout clones showed a marked reduction in sterol-induced HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: Following sterol addition, gp78/RNF145 double-knockout clones showed a marked (although still incomplete) reduction in sterol-induced HMGCR degradation (Figure 3F, compare lanes 7 + 8 with 9 –12).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The E3 ligase activity of RNF145 is critical for HMGCR ERAD.
claims.source: The E3 ligase activity of RNF145 is therefore critical for HMGCR ERAD.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the complementation experiment shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Wild type RNF145, but not the RNF145 RING domain mutant, rescued the block in sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR-Clover.
claims.source: The pronounced block in the sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR-Clover was at least partially rescued by expression of wild type, but not the RNF145 RING domain mutant (Figure 4B, compare blue to red histogram).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Endogenous RNF145 has a short half-life (~2 hr).
claims.source: Endogenous RNF145 has a short half-life (~2 hr) and displayed rapid, proteasome-mediated degradation (Figure 5A (i)), an observation confirmed in multiple cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Endogenous RNF145 displayed rapid, proteasome-mediated degradation.
claims.source: Endogenous RNF145 has a short half-life (~2 hr) and displayed rapid, proteasome-mediated degradation (Figure 5A (i)), an observation confirmed in multiple cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Endogenous gp78 shows little degradation over a 10 hr chase period.
claims.source: This rapid turnover of endogenous RNF145 contrasts sharply with the stability of endogenous gp78, which shows little degradation over the 10 hr chase period (Figure 5A (i)).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: RNF145 stability was unaffected by gp78.
claims.source: Although RNF145 and gp78 both target HMGCR for degradation, the two ligases did not appear to be co-regulated as RNF145 stability was unaffected by gp78 and vice-versa (Figure 5A (i, ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: gp78 stability was unaffected by RNF145.
claims.source: Although RNF145 and gp78 both target HMGCR for degradation, the two ligases did not appear to be co-regulated as RNF145 stability was unaffected by gp78 and vice-versa (Figure 5A (i, ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Endogenous RNF145 was stabilised by deletion of UBE2G2.
claims.source: However, endogenous RNF145 was stabilised by deletion of its cognate E2 enzyme UBE2G2 (Figure 5B), and, furthermore, the catalytically-inactive RING domain mutant expressed in RNF145-deficient cells (ΔRNF145 #4 + RNF145-V5 (mut)) exhibited greater abundance at steady-state compared with its wild type counterpart (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The catalytically-inactive RING domain mutant of RNF145 exhibited greater abundance at steady-state compared with its wild type counterpart.
claims.source: However, endogenous RNF145 was stabilised by deletion of its cognate E2 enzyme UBE2G2 (Figure 5B), and, furthermore, the catalytically-inactive RING domain mutant expressed in RNF145-deficient cells (ΔRNF145 #4 + RNF145-V5 (mut)) exhibited greater abundance at steady-state compared with its wild type counterpart (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claims.claim: RNF145 is intrinsically unstable and rapidly turned over in an auto-regulatory manner.
claims.source: Together these data show that RNF145 is intrinsically unstable and rapidly turned over in an auto-regulatory manner.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data on RNF145 stability.

claims.claim: Sterol depletion induced RNF145 mRNA expression (~2.99 ± 0.65 fold increase).
claims.source: Since RNF145 is rapidly turned over, we aimed to determine whether RNF145 gene transcription was sterol-responsive. Sterol depletion induced RNF145 (~2.99 ± 0.65 fold increase, p=0.0009) mRNA expression as well as HMGCR (~12.26 ± 3.16 fold increase, p=0.0004) mRNA expression (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Sterol depletion induced HMGCR mRNA expression (~12.26 ± 3.16 fold increase).
claims.source: Since RNF145 is rapidly turned over, we aimed to determine whether RNF145 gene transcription was sterol-responsive. Sterol depletion induced RNF145 (~2.99 ± 0.65 fold increase, p=0.0009) mRNA expression as well as HMGCR (~12.26 ± 3.16 fold increase, p=0.0004) mRNA expression (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Accumulation of endogenous RNF145 was suppressed following the addition of cholesterol to the starvation media.
claims.source: This accumulation of endogenous RNF145 was suppressed following the addition of methyl beta-cyclodextrin (MBCD)-complexed cholesterol (Chol/MBCD) to the starvation media (Figure 5D), whereas gp78 abundance remained unaltered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: gp78 abundance remained unaltered following the addition of cholesterol to the starvation media.
claims.source: This accumulation of endogenous RNF145 was suppressed following the addition of methyl beta-cyclodextrin (MBCD)-complexed cholesterol (Chol/MBCD) to the starvation media (Figure 5D), whereas gp78 abundance remained unaltered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: RNF145 is a sterol-regulated E3 ubiquitin ligase whose expression is dependent on the cellular sterol status.
claims.source: RNF145 is therefore a unique, sterol-regulated E3 ubiquitin ligase whose expression is dependent on the cellular sterol status.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data on RNF145 transcriptional regulation.

claims.claim: In sterol-replete but not sterol-deplete conditions, endogenous HMGCR co-immunoprecipitates epitope-tagged RNF145.
claims.source: We found that in sterol-replete but not sterol-deplete conditions, endogenous HMGCR co-immunoprecipitates both epitope-tagged RNF145 (Figure 6A, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C lane three for relative RNF145-V5 levels upon reconstitution), as well as endogenous RNF145 (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: In sterol-replete but not sterol-deplete conditions, endogenous HMGCR co-immunoprecipitates endogenous RNF145.
claims.source: We found that in sterol-replete but not sterol-deplete conditions, endogenous HMGCR co-immunoprecipitates both epitope-tagged RNF145 (Figure 6A, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C lane three for relative RNF145-V5 levels upon reconstitution), as well as endogenous RNF145 (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: RNF145 showed a sterol-dependent interaction with Insig-1.
claims.source: Under these conditions, RNF145 showed a clear, sterol-dependent interaction with Insig-1, correlating with RNF145's association with HMGCR (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Endogenous RNF145 is not continually bound to Insig-1, but associates with Insig-1 in a sterol-dependent manner.
claims.source: Importantly, endogenous RNF145 is not, therefore, continually bound to Insig-1, but, like HMGCR, associates with Insig-1 in a sterol-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: Binding of RNF145 to Insig-1 was HMGCR-independent.
claims.source: Binding of RNF145 to Insig-1 was HMGCR-independent (Figure 6D) and, in the absence of Insigs, RNF145 was unable to bind HMGCR (Figure 6E, see Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C for generation of Insig-1+2 knockout cells).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: In the absence of Insigs, RNF145 was unable to bind HMGCR.
claims.source: Binding of RNF145 to Insig-1 was HMGCR-independent (Figure 6D) and, in the absence of Insigs, RNF145 was unable to bind HMGCR (Figure 6E, see Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C for generation of Insig-1+2 knockout cells).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Insigs are indispensable for the interaction between RNF145 and HMGCR.
claims.source: Insigs are therefore indispensable for the interaction between RNF145 and HMGCR.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: Insig proteins play a central role as scaffolds in the sterol-induced engagement of HMGCR by RNF145.
claims.source: These findings emphasize the central role of Insig proteins as scaffolds in the sterol-induced engagement of HMGCR by RNF145.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: Ablation of UBE2G2 in RNF145/gp78 double-knockout cells exacerbated the sterol-dependent degradation defect.
claims.source: Furthermore, ablation of UBE2G2 in RNF145/gp78 double-knockout cells exacerbated the sterol-dependent degradation defect (Figure 7A (iv)), predicting the role for an additional E3 ubiquitin ligase(s) utilising UBE2G2 in HMGCR degradation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: An additional E3 ubiquitin ligase(s) utilising UBE2G2 is involved in HMGCR degradation.
claims.source: Furthermore, ablation of UBE2G2 in RNF145/gp78 double-knockout cells exacerbated the sterol-dependent degradation defect (Figure 7A (iv)), predicting the role for an additional E3 ubiquitin ligase(s) utilising UBE2G2 in HMGCR degradation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: Loss of TRC8 had no effect on HMGCR-Clover expression.
claims.source: While the loss of TRC8 had no effect on HMGCR-Clover expression, the loss of Hrd1 in RNF145/gp78 double-knockout cells increased steady-state HMGCR-Clover expression and caused a complete block in the sterol-accelerated degradation of HMGCR-Clover (Figure 7B (ii), Figure 7—figure supplement 1A for validation with individual independent sgRNAs).

results.result: The authors generated an HMGCR-Clover reporter cell line by fusing Clover fluorescent protein to the C-terminus of endogenous HMGCR. This reporter is dynamic and cholesterol-sensitive, showing ~25-fold increase upon sterol depletion and ~80% decrease within 2 hours of sterol repletion. The reporter is stabilized by proteasome, p97/VCP, or HMGCR enzymatic inhibition, and its degradation is Insig-dependent with Insig-1 being dominant over Insig-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C50 collectively demonstrate successful generation and validation of the HMGCR-Clover reporter. The data show appropriate ER localization (C50), sterol-dependent regulation (C38-C40), proteasome-dependent degradation (C42-C44), and Insig-dependence (C45-C49). Multiple complementary approaches (flow cytometry, immunoblotting, microscopy, genetic validation) provide converging evidence.

results.result: A genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen identified RNF145 as an E3 ligase required for HMGCR degradation, along with known components UBE2G2, AUP1, and Insig-1/2. RNF145 depletion caused a small but reproducible decrease in HMGCR-Clover degradation, suggesting involvement of additional ligases.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C61 describe the genome-wide screen results with appropriate validation. The identification of known components (C52, C53, C55) validates the screening approach, while RNF145 emerges as a novel E3 ligase (C51, C56). The modest phenotype upon RNF145 depletion (C60) is appropriately interpreted as suggesting redundancy (C61), motivating the subsequent targeted screen.

results.result: A targeted ubiquitome CRISPR/Cas9 screen in RNF145-deficient cells identified gp78 as a second E3 ligase for HMGCR degradation. Loss of gp78 alone had no effect, but combined loss of RNF145 and gp78 resulted in significant accumulation of HMGCR-Clover and inability to degrade it upon sterol addition, demonstrating partial functional redundancy between the two ligases.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 demonstrate a well-designed genetic approach to identify redundant ligases. The targeted screen in RNF145-deficient background (C62) successfully identified gp78 (C62), and the epistasis analysis showing no effect of gp78 alone (C63) but strong effect in combination with RNF145 (C66) provides compelling evidence for redundancy (C67-C68). The conclusion that gp78 was not a false-negative from the initial screen (C64) is logically sound.

results.result: The redundancy between RNF145 and gp78 in HMGCR degradation was confirmed using endogenous wild-type HMGCR. Loss of gp78 alone did not affect HMGCR degradation, but combined loss of gp78 and RNF145 resulted in significant rescue of steady-state HMGCR and marked reduction in sterol-induced degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 validate the findings from the HMGCR-Clover reporter using endogenous HMGCR by immunoblotting. This addresses potential concerns about reporter artifacts and confirms the phenotypes observed with the fluorescent reporter apply to native HMGCR. The data in multiple independent clones strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: The E3 ligase activity of RNF145 is critical for HMGCR degradation. Wild-type RNF145, but not a catalytically-inactive RING domain mutant, rescued the block in sterol-induced degradation of HMGCR-Clover in RNF145/gp78 double-knockout cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 demonstrate that RNF145's enzymatic activity is required for its function in HMGCR degradation through a complementation experiment. The use of a RING domain mutant (C552A, H554A) is appropriate for testing E3 ligase activity, and the rescue by wild-type but not mutant RNF145 provides strong evidence for the requirement of catalytic activity.

results.result: Endogenous RNF145 has a short half-life (~2 hours) and undergoes rapid, proteasome-mediated degradation in an auto-regulatory manner dependent on UBE2G2. This contrasts with the stable gp78, and the two ligases are not co-regulated. The catalytically-inactive RING mutant of RNF145 exhibited greater steady-state abundance than wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C81 characterize RNF145 stability through cycloheximide chase experiments in multiple cell lines. The data show RNF145 is intrinsically unstable (C74-C75), contrasting with stable gp78 (C76), and that the ligases are not co-regulated (C77-C78). The stabilization by UBE2G2 deletion (C79) and increased abundance of the RING mutant (C80) support auto-regulation (C81). The experiments are well-controlled and conclusions appropriately drawn.

results.result: RNF145 is a sterol-regulated E3 ubiquitin ligase whose expression is dependent on cellular sterol status. Sterol depletion induced RNF145 mRNA expression (~3-fold increase, p=0.0009) and protein accumulation, which was suppressed by cholesterol addition. In contrast, gp78 abundance remained unaltered by sterol status.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 demonstrate sterol-dependent transcriptional regulation of RNF145 through qPCR (C82) and immunoblotting (C84). The statistical significance is reported (C82), and the contrast with gp78 (C85) highlights RNF145's unique regulation. The conclusion that RNF145 is sterol-regulated (C86) is well-supported by the data, though the mechanism of transcriptional regulation could be further explored.

results.result: Endogenous RNF145 shows sterol-dependent interaction with HMGCR and Insig-1. RNF145 binds Insig-1 in a sterol-dependent and HMGCR-independent manner, and in the absence of Insigs, RNF145 cannot bind HMGCR. This demonstrates that Insig proteins are indispensable scaffolds for the sterol-induced engagement of HMGCR by RNF145.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C94 establish the molecular mechanism of RNF145 recruitment to HMGCR through co-immunoprecipitation experiments. The sterol-dependence of RNF145-HMGCR interaction (C87-C88), sterol-dependent RNF145-Insig-1 interaction (C89-C90), HMGCR-independence of RNF145-Insig-1 binding (C91), and requirement for Insigs in RNF145-HMGCR interaction (C92) collectively support the scaffold model (C93-C94). The experiments in UBE2G2 knockout cells to increase RNF145 levels is a clever approach to overcome detection limitations.

results.result: In the absence of both RNF145 and gp78, Hrd1 partially regulates HMGCR degradation. Loss of Hrd1 in RNF145/gp78 double-knockout cells increased steady-state HMGCR-Clover and caused complete block in sterol-accelerated degradation. Hrd1 depletion had no effect alone or with either RNF145 or gp78 individually, and TRC8 showed no role in HMGCR degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C105 reveal a third ligase (Hrd1) involved in HMGCR degradation through systematic epistasis analysis. The exacerbation of the degradation defect by UBE2G2 ablation in double knockouts (C95) predicted additional ligase involvement (C96). The specific requirement for loss of both RNF145 and gp78 to reveal Hrd1's role (C98-C99, C101, C105) demonstrates a hierarchical redundancy. The exclusion of TRC8 (C97, C102-C103) with functional validation addresses prior literature. The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

results.result: Combined loss of RNF145 and gp78 showed dramatic reduction in HMGCR ubiquitination, but complete loss required depletion of all three ligases (RNF145, gp78, and Hrd1). UBE2G2 depletion also caused marked decrease in HMGCR ubiquitination.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 provide direct biochemical evidence for the roles of the three ligases in HMGCR ubiquitination. The graded effect (dramatic reduction with two ligases, complete loss with three) supports the genetic data and demonstrates that all three ligases contribute to HMGCR ubiquitination. The UBE2G2 result (C108) confirms all ligases use this E2 enzyme.

results.result: Three E3 ubiquitin ligases—RNF145, gp78, and Hrd1—are together responsible for HMGCR degradation. RNF145 and gp78 are partially redundant primary ligases, while Hrd1 can compensate only in the absence of both RNF145 and gp78, and in no other combination.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 summarize the main findings of the study. The conclusion that three ligases are responsible (C109) is supported by the comprehensive genetic and biochemical data. The characterization of partial redundancy between RNF145 and gp78 (C110) and the specific compensatory role of Hrd1 (C111-C112) accurately reflect the experimental results. This represents a major advance in understanding HMGCR regulation.

results.result: The genome-wide screen successfully identified many components known to be required for sterol-accelerated HMGCR degradation (Insig-1/2, UBE2G2, AUP1, FAF2), validating the genetic approach.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 provides important validation of the screening methodology by demonstrating recovery of known components. This increases confidence in the novel findings (RNF145) and addresses potential concerns about false negatives. The statement is supported by the screen data and cited literature.

results.result: The introduction establishes the biological context and controversy regarding HMGCR regulation. HMGCR is the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis and the target of statins. It is regulated transcriptionally by SREBPs and post-transcriptionally by sterol-accelerated degradation. The identity of the E3 ligase(s) responsible for mammalian HMGCR degradation has been controversial, with conflicting reports about roles for gp78, TRC8, and Hrd1.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C36 provide established background knowledge with appropriate citations. These claims set up the scientific problem addressed by the study—the controversial identity of E3 ligases for HMGCR degradation. The conflicting prior reports (C30-C36) justify the need for the current study. All claims are appropriately cited or represent well-established knowledge.

results.result: RNF145 harbors a YLYF motif at its N-terminus similar to the YIYF motif in the sterol-sensing domains of SCAP and HMGCR that is required for Insig binding. RNF145 shares 27% amino acid identity with TRC8. AUP1 recruits UBE2G2 to lipid droplets and membrane E3 ligases.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C57-C59 provide structural and functional context for RNF145 and related proteins. The YLYF motif observation (C57-C58) is important for predicting RNF145's interaction with Insigs, which is later experimentally validated. The sequence similarity to TRC8 (C56) and AUP1's function (C54) are appropriately cited. These claims provide important context but are not primary findings.

results.result: The abstract summarizes the main findings: RNF145 and gp78 independently coordinate HMGCR ubiquitination and degradation; RNF145 is a sterol-responsive ER-resident E3 ligase that is unstable but accumulates following sterol depletion; sterol addition triggers RNF145 recruitment to HMGCR via Insigs; and Hrd1 partially regulates HMGCR in the absence of both RNF145 and gp78.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C12 are summary statements from the abstract that are supported by the detailed experimental results described in other claim groups. These represent accurate summaries of the major findings that are substantiated by the data presented in the manuscript.

results.result: The Discussion speculates on the biological significance of ligase redundancy in HMGCR regulation. Possible explanations include: the central role of HMGCR requiring fail-safe mechanisms; different Insig-associated complexes co-existing in the ER; gp78 providing basal control with RNF145 fine-tuning; and conformational changes in HMGCR under sterol-rich conditions being recognized by Hrd1's quality control pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119, C123, C125 are speculative interpretations about why multiple ligases regulate HMGCR. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the data and cited literature, they are explicitly presented as speculation and are not directly tested. The speculation is appropriate for a Discussion section but does not constitute supported findings.

results.result: The Discussion cites prior literature showing that liver-specific ablation of gp78 in mice increased hepatocyte HMGCR levels, while gp78 knockout MEFs showed no impairment in HMGCR degradation. Hrd1's recognized function is ubiquitination of misfolded ER proteins. In yeast, ligand-induced local misfolding ('mallostery') in Hmg2p is a suggested mode of Hrd1p recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C122, C124 cite prior literature to provide context for the current findings. These are appropriately cited and help interpret the results, particularly regarding tissue-specific effects (C120-C121) and potential mechanisms for Hrd1 involvement (C122, C124). These represent accurate reporting of prior work.
